lead: This unit covers how applications talk over a network. After reading, the student can design a simple client‑server program, resolve host names, and understand basic web, file and mail services.
about: Unit 6 has seven chapters. 6.1 introduces client‑server and peer‑to‑peer models. 6.2 shows how to create TCP and UDP sockets. 6.3 explains DNS name resolution. 6.4 covers HTTP request‑response. 6.5 describes FTP file transfer. 6.6 details SMTP mail sending. 6.7 gives a starter view of network security and secure sockets. Each chapter builds on the previous one, using the same socket concepts and the same layered view of the Internet.

chapters.idea: Client‑server and peer‑to‑peer are the two main application architectures.
chapters.depth: Define client, server, peer, request‑response, stateful vs stateless. Give examples: web browser (client‑server) and video sharing app (peer‑to‑peer). Mention that some syllabi call this "network application architectures". Keep discussion to logical roles, not NAT details.

figure.title: Application models
figure.aria: Shows a client contacting a server and two peers exchanging data directly.

chapters.example: A Chennai user checks train status on a mobile app (client → server). The app sends 2 KB request, receives 1 KB JSON in 150 ms. The same user shares a 5 MB video with a friend using a peer‑to‑peer link that takes 2 s.
chapters.trap: Writing that the server initiates the connection in a peer‑to‑peer scenario.
chapters.leave: NAT traversal and firewall effects are covered in later security chapter.

chapters.idea: Sockets provide the programming interface for TCP and UDP communication.
chapters.depth: Define socket, IP address, port (0‑65535). Explain TCP socket steps: socket(), bind(), listen(), accept(), send(), recv(). Explain UDP steps: socket(), sendto(), recvfrom(). Mention blocking vs non‑blocking. Some syllabi list "TCP sockets" and "UDP sockets". Keep code snippets short.

figure.aria: Shows the three‑way TCP handshake followed by a data exchange.

chapters.example: Two phones exchange the message "Hi" (2 bytes) using UDP on port 5000. Each datagram arrives in 100 ms.
chapters.trap: Using send() instead of sendto() for a UDP socket.
chapters.leave: TLS/SSL encryption is treated in the security chapter.

chapters.idea: DNS translates human readable names to IP addresses.
chapters.depth: Describe DNS hierarchy, zones, and resource records (A, CNAME, MX). Explain recursive and iterative queries, UDP port 53, fallback to TCP for large answers. Mention caching TTL. Some syllabi list "Structure of the DNS" and "Dynamic Update"; treat dynamic update as an advanced topic (only a few universities teach it).

figure.aria: Tree shows the DNS lookup path from the root to www.irctc.co.in.

chapters.example: Resolve www.irctc.co.in from Chennai. Query root (30 ms) → get .in NS. Query .in (30 ms) → get irctc.co.in NS. Query irctc.co.in (30 ms) → receive A record 203.197.0.1. Total 90 ms.
chapters.trap: Confusing an authoritative server with a recursive resolver.
chapters.leave: DNSSEC and advanced dynamic updates are left for the security chapter.

chapters.idea: HTTP enables web browsers to request and receive web resources.
chapters.depth: Define URL parts, methods (GET, POST), status codes, headers, and statelessness. Mention persistent connections (HTTP/1.1). Some syllabi list HTTP under Application layer protocols. Treat HTTPS as an advanced addition (few universities teach it).

figure.aria: Shows a simple HTTP GET request and the server's response.

chapters.example: A laptop requests http://example.com/index.html. The server returns a 1.2 KB HTML page after 120 ms. Header includes Content‑Type: text/html.
chapters.trap: Assuming POST is safe like GET; exam may ask which methods are idempotent.
chapters.leave: TLS encryption for HTTPS is covered in the security chapter.

chapters.idea: FTP moves files using separate control and data connections.
chapters.depth: Explain FTP commands (USER, PASS, RETR, STOR), ports (21 control, 20 data for active mode, server‑chosen port for passive). Describe active vs passive mode and firewall impact. Some syllabi list FTP as an Application layer protocol.

figure.title: FTP connections
figure.aria: Shows the client’s control connection to port 21 and the data connection in passive mode.

chapters.example: Upload a 5 MB PDF using passive FTP. Data rate 2 MB/s, so transfer time = 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 s plus 0.2 s command overhead.
chapters.trap: Thinking the client opens port 20 in active mode; actually the server does.
chapters.leave: Secure FTP (FTPS, SFTP) is left for the security chapter.

chapters.idea: SMTP moves email from sender to recipient using a store‑and‑forward model.
chapters.depth: Define SMTP, ports 25, 587 (STARTTLS), 465 (TLS). Explain roles: MUA, MTA, MDA. Show basic commands: HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA, QUIT. Mention MIME for attachments. Some syllabi list POP3/IMAP but focus on SMTP here.

figure.aria: Shows the flow of an email from the sender’s client through two SMTP servers to the recipient’s mailbox.

chapters.example: Student sends a 200 KB image to a professor. SMTP transaction (HELO, MAIL, RCPT, DATA) takes 0.8 s over a 10 Mbps link.
chapters.trap: Assuming SMTP directly deposits the message into the recipient’s inbox without intermediate servers.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 4 (HTTP) for similar request‑response pattern and Chapter 2 (sockets).
chapters.leave: POP3/IMAP retrieval and advanced authentication are left for later study.

chapters.idea: Basic security concepts protect application‑layer traffic.
chapters.depth: Define firewall, NAT, encryption, SSL/TLS handshake, authentication, common attacks (eavesdropping, spoofing, DoS). Mention that only a few universities teach full TLS details (advanced). Show how HTTPS adds a TLS layer over HTTP and how FTPS adds it over FTP.

figure.title: TLS protected channel
figure.aria: Shows a client and server establishing a TLS handshake before exchanging encrypted data.

chapters.example: A user logs into a banking website over HTTPS. The TLS handshake uses 2 round trips (30 ms each) = 60 ms overhead, then the login request (0.1 ms) is encrypted.
chapters.trap: Believing that using HTTP alone prevents man‑in‑the‑middle attacks.
chapters.prereq: All previous chapters, especially socket programming.
chapters.leave: Deep cryptographic algorithms and PKI are marked as advanced and not covered here.
